The voice and face look like hers, but there’s nothing on the school website. I check first. <strong>Circolare pubblicata sul sito uf: Notice published on the school’s official website and in the online register, opened by you: “Tomorrow lessons start at 9:00 due to a staff meeting.” I trust it. It’s the primary, official source, checked directly on the school’s own channel.
<strong>Vocale inoltrato decine di volte: Voice note forwarded dozens of times in the class chat: “It’s all true, my friend’s cousin who works at the hospital sent it to me!” I check first. A chain-forwarded voice note with no name, date or checkable source is classic rumour-mill material.
<strong>Screenshot di un articolo con un: Screenshot of an article with a sensational headline, cropped with no date, no author and no link to the original page. I check first. A screenshot can be doctored in seconds: look for the original piece on the publication’s website.
<strong>Avviso di allerta meteo con data: Weather warning with today’s date and time, read directly on the official Civil Protection or municipal website. I trust it. It has an accountable public body, an exact date and time, and is checked at the source.
<strong>Telefonata da un numero sconosci: Call from an unknown number: a voice identical to your mother’s says she broke her phone and asks for an urgent bank transfer. I check first. A few seconds of audio are enough to clone a voice with AI: hang up and call back on her usual number (or ask for the family secret word).
<strong>Foto drammatica di un incendio i: Dramatic photo of a city fire with 50,000 shares: a search shows the picture is from four years ago in another country. I check first. A real photo that is old or out of context misleads just like a fake: shares don’t measure truth.
<strong>Rapporto con data di pubblicazio: Report with publication date, methodology note and downloadable data, read on the national statistics institute’s official portal. I trust it. It states who collected the data, when and how, on a verifiable institutional source.
Perché cercare a occhio i difetti di un: Why is spotting visual glitches in a video (hands, shadows, lips) no longer enough to tell if it was made with AI?
<strong>Dove portare la classe:</strong>: Where to take the class: Generative models keep improving and visual glitches fade away. The only check that holds up over time is outside the video: tracing the original source, date, provenance credentials (such as C2PA) and confirmation on independent channels.
«Non l’ho creato io, l’ho solo inoltrato: “I didn’t make it, I only forwarded it to the group”: why does that excuse fail, both humanly and legally?
<strong>Dove portare la classe:</strong>: Where to take the class: Without people forwarding it, a fake goes nowhere. Sharing gives it reach and credibility among your contacts; moreover, in Italy, Article 612-quater of the Criminal Code (Law 132/2025) also punishes anyone who passes on, publishes or spreads AI-falsified images, videos or voices without consent, causing unjust harm.
Dal 2 agosto 2026 l’articolo 50 dell’AI: From 2 August 2026 Article 50 of the EU AI Act requires deepfakes to be disclosed. Why do we still need to check for ourselves?
<strong>Dove portare la classe:</strong>: Where to take the class: Because the rule binds those who follow the law, whereas someone running a scam or a disinformation campaign will never add an “AI-generated” label. Labels help, but the reader remains the final filter.
